vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: outlook
Version: 1.3.0

The skill is classified as suspicious due to a path traversal vulnerability in the `scripts/outlook-mail.sh` file, specifically within the `download` command. This vulnerability allows an attacker to write email attachment content to arbitrary file paths on the agent's filesystem by crafting a malicious attachment name (e.g., `../../.bashrc`). While not clear evidence of intentional malicious behavior by the skill developer, this flaw provides a powerful primitive for a malicious prompt to exploit, potentially leading to persistence or arbitrary code execution. Additionally, the skill requests broad permissions (Mail.ReadWrite, Mail.Send, Calendars.ReadWrite) which, while aligned with its stated purpose, represent high-risk capabilities.

llm.summary: This Outlook skill mostly does what it says, but it asks for durable read/write/send access to mail and calendar data and has under-scoped handling of tokens, destructive actions, and attachment downloads.

dimensions.detail: Most local file access is tied to the Outlook configuration directory, but attachment download writes decoded attachment content to a caller-supplied path combined with the attachment name without path normalization, traversal checks, symlink checks, or no-clobber protection.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The automated setup creates an Azure app registration, adds Mail.ReadWrite, Mail.Send, Calendars.ReadWrite, and User.Read delegated permissions, creates a two-year client secret, and stores OAuth material locally. It also prints a curl-to-sudo-bash Azure CLI install suggestion when Azure CLI is missing; this is not auto-executed, but it is unsafe setup guidance.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill exposes high-impact operations such as send, reply, forward, delete, bulk-delete, delete-folder, calendar update, and calendar delete without documented confirmation, preview, or rollback safeguards. The behavior is command-driven rather than hidden, but the scope is broad for an agent-invoked email/calendar skill.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The skill stores client credentials and access/refresh tokens in ~/.outlook-mcp, uses offline_access for ongoing access, refreshes tokens from disk, and includes a command that prints the bearer access token to stdout. chmod 600 is used during setup, but the persistence and token-printing behavior remain high-impact.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: The main purpose is coherent: the artifacts include mail and calendar scripts using Microsoft Graph for reading, searching, sending, modifying, and deleting Outlook data. Some additional mail capabilities, including forwarding, drafts, bulk delete, folder deletion, categorization, and attachment download, are present in the script help but are not clearly listed in the main skill usage section.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Install only if you are comfortable granting this skill read/write/send access to your Outlook mail and read/write access to your calendar with refresh-token persistence. Avoid running the displayed curl-to-sudo-bash Azure CLI installer, do not use the token-printing command in logged agent sessions, confirm any send/delete/bulk/folder/calendar action yourself, and treat downloaded attachments as able to overwrite local files unless you choose a safe empty directory.
llm.findings:
[TP4] expected: The package contains both mail and calendar scripts, so the broad email/calendar description is mostly supported. The stronger artifact-backed issue is under-disclosure of several extra mail commands in the script help, not a complete description-to-implementation mismatch.
[PE3] expected: Local OAuth token use is expected for this Graph integration, but plaintext refresh-capable credentials in ~/.outlook-mcp and the documented token-printing command are material credential-handling concerns.
[SC2] unexpected: The Azure CLI prerequisite message recommends piping a remote installer to sudo bash. It is only displayed guidance, not automatic execution, but it is unnecessary and unsafe for a skill setup path.
[TM2] unexpected: The command-chaining concern is supported by the same displayed curl-to-sudo-bash installer suggestion; it does not prove malicious behavior, but it warrants review.
[LP3] expected: Shell scripts are the declared implementation mechanism, but the artifact does not define narrow agent tool boundaries around which scripts and arguments may be run.
[SQP-1] expected: Broad Outlook, inbox, email, and calendar triggers fit the skill purpose, but they can route privacy-sensitive account operations from common user requests.
[SQP-2] expected: Delete, send, reply, and calendar mutation commands are purpose-aligned, but the artifacts do not document confirmation requirements for destructive or outbound actions.
[RA2] expected: Persistent app registration and refresh tokens are coherent with ongoing Outlook access, but they create durable mailbox and calendar authority that users must be able to revoke.
[PE2] expected: The sudo references are install-prerequisite guidance for jq and Azure CLI rather than privilege escalation inside the Outlook scripts; the Azure CLI curl-to-sudo guidance remains the material issue.
[T03] unexpected: The static finding is supported for the displayed Azure CLI install command. Because the skill does not run the remote installer automatically, this supports Review rather than malicious classification.
[T09] unexpected: The attachment download path handling can overwrite arbitrary user-writable files, and unsafe jq/JSON interpolation can manipulate Graph requests or break valid inputs. These are implementation flaws rather than evidence of intentional harm.
